newsitem.title: USA: IMF says Argentina should stick to currency board.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Argentina should stick to currency board.

text.p: Argentina should stick to the currency board system that has allowed it to achieve among the lowest inflation rates in the world, IMF chief economist Michael Mussa said Wednesday.

"I think that, at this stage, to stay the course is the right prescription for Argentine economic policy," Mussa said at a news conference on the International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook report.
A debate is growing in Argentina about the future of the currency board established by law in 1991 to end the peso's prolonged tumble against the dollar.

The system, which forces the Argentine central bank to back every peso in circulation with U.S. dollars, gold or bonds, restored confidence in the local currency and helped defeat a bout of hyperinflation.

However, pressured by a struggling recovery from last year's recession and record levels of unemployment, even some former staunch supporters of the currency board are starting to argue that it has outlived its purpose.

"This is an issue that needs to be evaluated on the basis of the medium term, rather than this month or this year," Mussa said in answer to a question on whether Argentina should keep or scrap its currency board.
The IMF's chief economist pointed out that under that exchange system, which effectively pegged the peso to the dollar, Argentina achieved its best economic performance in over six decades.
Before the 1995 Mexican peso crisis whipped its economy, Argentina GDP growth averaged about eight percent and it had brought inflation from over 5,000 percent to single digits.
Mussa added that Argentina's economy contracted by only half as much as Mexico's did last year, and that Argentine inflation fell while Mexican consumer prices rocketed.
"So if we are doing comparisons, there is no doubt that the Argentine economy survived the shock a great deal better," he said.

In its most recent report, the IMF forecast that Argentina's GDP would grow by about 2.5 percent this year after last year's 4.4 percent drop. Mexico's is due to rebound 3.5 percent this year after a 6.9 percent contraction in 1995.
The IMF also sees Argentine inflation falling to 0.3 percent this year from 3.2 percent in 1995, while Mexico's will likely end at around 34 percent, almost unchanged from last year's 35 percent.
"We now see clear evidence that the Argentine economy is recovering, and its inflation is essentially the lowest in the world," Mussa said.

"It will take some time, of course, for real wages and some sectors of the economy to recover, and unemployment remains high, but productivity growth has been strong and international competitiveness has improved," he added.
